summary: Deep dive on KV cache eviction and paging behavior under long-context workloads with heavy prefix reuse. Identified likely causes: hot-prefix thrashing, inadequate per-prefix quotas, long-lived KV entries from conversational stitching, and prefetch heuristics that overfetch. Agreed next steps to capture token-level telemetry, run a controlled on-prem benchmark, and propose config changes (adaptive TTL, per-prefix soft limits, sticky routing).
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-21 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Alex Johnson (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Lead ML Engineer - Lumos), Marta Ruiz (Infra), Evan Cho (SRE), Janelle Wu (PM)

[00:00] Alex: ok thanks everyone for joining, um we're here to dig into the cache behavior you flagged. i think priya and i can run through what our runtime sees and then we can go into the traces you shared.
[00:12] Samir: yeah thanks, appreciate it. to summarize — we're seeing periodic large tail latencies and occasional request failures when the conversational context grows beyond ~15k tokens. overall throughput drops and we see a lot of kv evictions.
[00:25] Priya: noted, and you said this is mostly on your production traffic or a mix?
[00:30] Marta: primarily production, yes. dev is fine. prod has spikes of reused session prefixes — several users end up hitting the same prefix keys and that seems to push other prefixes out.
[00:42] Priya: got it. so two dimensions: prefix reuse/hotspotting, and long-lived contexts causing large per-session kv entries. both can increase working set and cause spill/paging.
[00:55] Evan: when you say spill, are we talking disk paging inside the runtime or offloading to remote store? our monitoring shows our nodes hitting high memory and then kernel-level swap activity.
[01:05] Priya: in your traces we saw both. there's an internal spill path we call paging where the KV layer serializes less-recent entries and moves them to local SSD queue to reclaim GPU RAM. it's fast but when the working set is much larger than the local cache, the overhead becomes significant.
[01:20] Alex: important note — our paging path aims for sub-10ms per token for warmup but if you have bursty hot prefixes, the re-warm cost stacks.
[01:32] Samir: right, the warmup is killing us. we're seeing tokens queued and then long backpressure on the model runtime. is prefix reuse the primary root cause? or is it the prefetch policy?
[01:45] Priya: both. in many cases hot prefixes dominate the cache capacity. if prefetch heuristics are conservative they may underfetch and cause misses; if they're aggressive they overfetch and evict other useful prefixes. for your workload, the hot prefixes are relatively narrow but very frequent — they never age out, so they effectively steal slots.
[02:05] Janelle: what's a slot in this context? like a fixed kv entry size?
[02:09] Priya: good question. our KV is segmented — entries are variable size but we budget per-prefix soft quotas. a 'slot' here is conceptual: an allocation unit in the memory allocator. oversized long contexts consume many units.
[02:22] Alex: another nuance — quantization profiles affect memory per token for KV caches. if you're using lower-precision kernels to save model memory, the KV encoding can actually grow per-entry in some cases because of packing and alignment.
[02:35] Marta: oof we did enable 4-bit quantization for the model to reduce GPU footprint. could that be causing the cache behavior?
[02:40] Priya: it can. lower precision reduces model parameter memory but the KV cache encoding path currently quantizes separately; depending on the encoding, you might see higher transient working set during dequant/pack. it's not the primary cause but it's additive.
[02:55] Evan: can you explain prefix affinity / sticky routing — would that help?
[03:00] Priya: sure, sticky routing binds high-frequency prefixes to specific workers so they don't get sharded across hosts and evicted intermittently. it reduces cross-host warmup but at the cost of uneven load distribution and potential hot machine saturation.
[03:15] Samir: we could tolerate some imbalance if it stabilizes latency. our SLO is 99th < 250ms for user-facing calls. right now we breach that during peaks.
[03:26] Alex: tradeoffs — sticky helps tail but increases risk of node saturation; per-prefix quotas and soft eviction policies help fairness. adaptive TTL is another lever: hot prefixes get shorter soft TTLs only when global working set is constrained.
[03:39] Janelle: hmm what's 'soft TTL'?
[03:41] Priya: it's basically a hint-based expiry. we don't forcibly evict until we need capacity, but we deprioritize refreshes for entries beyond soft TTL. entries can be proactively checkpointed for faster warmup.
[03:55] Marta: checkpointing meaning saving a compact snapshot locally?
[03:58] Priya: exactly — compact, lossy snapshots for long-context stitch tokens that can be rehydrated faster than a full recompute.
[04:08] Evan: your previous note about prefetch heuristics — do you do prefix-aware prefetch or purely recency-based?
[04:14] Priya: we have multiple signals: recency, prefix hit frequency, user/session affinity, and a cost model that estimates warmup cost vs eviction cost. sometimes the cost model errs with narrow but persistent prefixes.
[04:27] Samir: our workload seems to have two classes: small interactive chats (few tokens) and long analytic conversations (20k+ tokens). the latter are rare but long-lived and keep entries around. could we quarantine long-context sessions to a separate pool?
[04:41] Priya: yes, a long-context pool is one of the suggested mitigations — isolate large stateful sessions so they don't compete with short interactive traffic. we can route them to dedicated workers with larger KV budgets.
[04:52] Alex: that'll require routing changes in your VPC setup if you're on Private — but it's doable.
[04:58] Marta: we're on Redwood Private in a VPC. any routing changes need to pass through our network team. latency between subnets matters.
[05:05] Priya: understood. we can propose sticky routing within the same AZ and avoid cross-AZ fetches.
[05:12] Evan: you mentioned 'quota per prefix' earlier — how strict is it?
[05:16] Priya: we support soft and hard quotas. soft means throttling refreshes; hard enforces eviction. often you want soft first to reduce user impact.
[05:25] Samir: do you have examples of values other customers used?
[05:28] Priya: yes — for similar subscription/chat workloads, customers set soft quotas around 3-5MB per prefix and hard quotas at 8-12MB, with adaptive tiers based on SLA. but that depends on tokenization and embedding size.
[05:42] Alex: we should run an experiment with your token stats to propose numbers.
[05:45] Samir: attached in the deck is token distribution per session — the top 2% prefixes account for 40% of hits.
[05:52] Priya: that exactly matches hotspot behavior. in addition to per-prefix quotas we recommend: hot-prefix pinning, long-context pool, and prefetch TTL tuning.
[06:03] Janelle: any quick wins we can do without infra changes?
[06:05] Priya: yes — reduce prefetch window for low-frequency prefixes, enable soft quotas, and adjust KV garbage collector aggressiveness. those are config flips and low-risk.
[06:15] Marta: can you define "prefetch window" in our config terms?
[06:18] Priya: it's the number of future tokens we maintain a KV warmup for. bigger window reduces misses for predictable contexts but consumes memory. set it smaller for infrequent prefixes.
[06:29] Evan: question on telemetry: what exact traces do you need? we can produce flame graphs, perf counters, and packet captures.
[06:36] Priya: start with token-level hit/miss logs, prefix ID mapping, allocation sizes per entry, and periodic heap snapshots. a 3-day capture on a representative peak window is ideal.
[06:46] Alex: we'll also need the hot-prefix list and sample session IDs so we can replay traces in our test harness.
[06:52] Samir: ok we'll extract and share that.
[06:55] [07:00] Priya: quick aside — we saw in your logs that some prefixes get reused across accounts because of a client-side session reuse bug. could you instrument on the client to validate?
[07:12] Samir: hmm that's possible. i'll have the frontend team check session cookie reuse. good catch.
[07:18] Janelle: regarding compliance and VPC, we need to ensure KMS integration and audit logs remain intact if you suggest routing changes or pinned workers. any impact?
[07:27] Alex: no changes to KMS, but when we pin prefixes to dedicated hosts in private deployments we still keep KMS calls local. we'll share our network diagram and SAML flow.
[07:36] Marta: please send SOC2 docs as well, our security team will want that before larger experiments.
[07:40] Alex: will do.
[07:43] [08:00] Priya: let's walk through an example trace (Samir's sample).
[07:50] Samir: sure i'm sharing screen...
[08:00] Priya: (reviewing) here's a hot prefix with repeated small requests; notice KV miss spikes align with bursts of long-context sessions — the runtime attempts to prefetch a large window that causes eviction of other active prefixes, then the other requests pay the warmup cost.
[08:18] Evan: i see the backpressure pattern at t+45s where the request queue length jumps. that correlates with kernel swap spike at host level.
[08:25] Priya: exactly. recommended mitigations here: cap prefetch size for low-frequency prefixes, enable soft quotas, introduce per-worker hot-prefix pinning, and add a background async warmup for likely next-prefixes (probabilistic prefetch).
[08:40] Samir: about probabilistic prefetch — does that increase wasted work?
[08:44] Priya: yes if not tuned. that's why we combine it with a cost model: only prefetch when expected warmup benefit > eviction cost. we can run an offline sim with your distributions.
[08:56] Alex: another practical option is to tune the batching window. if you increase batch size you'll improve throughput but tail latency might worsen. for your user-facing interactive SLOs, we usually run with smaller max-batch and aggressive routing for short chats and larger batches on background analytic flows.
[09:12] Samir: okay so the plan could be: isolate long-context flows into separate queue with larger batch tolerance and separate KV pool. interactive flows stay low-latency.
[09:22] Priya: yes that mirrors what other customers do; we've seen 30-40% reduction in tail latencies after separation.
[09:30] Marta: what about disk-backed paging tuning? are there knobs to make rehydration faster?
[09:35] Priya: you can adjust serialization format (we have a "compact" snapshot), parallelize rehydration threads, and use NVMe local SSDs. also ensure the OS swappiness is tuned.
[09:47] Evan: can Redwood's runtime detect excessive swap and change behavior? like throttle prefetch?
[09:52] Priya: we have a reactive controller we can enable: when host-level memory pressure crosses threshold, runtime will shrink prefetch window and prioritize serving live requests. it's been stable in our tests.
[10:05] Samir: how invasive is enabling that controller? config switch?
[10:08] Priya: it's a config flag and a minor agent bump; no restarts needed in most cases.
[10:14] Alex: we'll include that in the recommended changes to try first.
[10:18] Janelle: timeline?
[10:20] Alex: propose: this week — telemetry capture and hot-prefix export; next week — Redwood runs replay in our harness and returns a config proposal; following week — pilot on-prem with dedicated pool.
[10:30] Samir: sounds reasonable.
[10:32] [11:00] Priya: quick note about metrics — please send us the distribution of tokens per request and per-session, and the KV entry size histogram. with those we'll simulate cost model changes.
[10:44] Marta: we'll extract those and post to the shared drive.
[10:47] Evan: any blockers on our side to the recommended non-intrusive flips? soft quotas and prefetch window reduction?
[10:52] Marta: no blockers, those are config-only. we can flip in a canary and monitor.
[10:56] Alex: great. last questions?
[11:00] Samir: two things — will any of these changes affect model quality? and what's the impact of quantization adjustments?
[11:07] Priya: prefretch/eviction changes won't alter model logits. quantization can, but we recommend running model-quality evals with a small cohort in parallel if you change quantization. for KV pack/unpack changes we have regression tests but still recommend smoke testing.
[11:20] Alex: ok, wrap-up — action items we'll send in the follow-up. thanks everyone.
[11:26] Janelle: thanks all.

Meeting end.

Notes (auto things):
